explanation_text: On a backstrap loom, threads are counted in groups of ten, and the position of a thread in the row decides what it becomes in the cloth. Just as each digit's place gives it value, each thread's position shapes the woven pattern.
image_prompt: Illustrate a backstrap loom with warp threads bundled in groups of ten, each group labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how position shapes the cloth.

explanation_text: When you pour more corn into a bamboo storage basket, the total rises; when you take some out to cook, it falls. This mirrors addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: Show a bamboo grain basket being filled with corn, then a portion being removed, with totals marked beside it.

explanation_text: The sani dance lines up dancers in equal rows, so counting rows times dancers per row is multiplication. Splitting the dancers into equal teams shows division.
image_prompt: Display sani dancers standing in even rows, showing equal grouping (multiplication) and even sharing (division).

explanation_text: When festival dancers join hands in pairs, the group is even. If one dancer is left over, the group is odd.
image_prompt: Show festival dancers holding hands in pairs, with one single dancer standing alone at the end to represent an odd number.

yi_culture: Dance steps of the sani dance
explanation_text: The sani dance follows a repeated rhythm where dancers step on every second or third beat, like counting by 2s or 3s. The repeating step pattern is a number pattern.
image_prompt: Show footprints along a dance floor marking every third step to illustrate skip counting.

explanation_text: Comparing two baskets filled with different amounts of buckwheat shows which is greater and which is smaller, just like comparing numbers.
image_prompt: Show several grain baskets with different amounts of buckwheat, using > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: When a family prepares for the long street banquet, they estimate how much grain each table needs, rounding to a convenient amount. Estimation and rounding make planning faster.
image_prompt: Show a cook estimating rice portions for the long street banquet, with rounded amounts labeled.

explanation_text: When a buckwheat pancake is shared equally among the family, each person receives a fraction of the whole. The equal parts are fractions.
image_prompt: Show a buckwheat pancake cut into equal wedges, each labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: A buckwheat pancake cut into 2 halves or 4 quarters still makes one whole pancake. Halves and quarters of the same pancake are equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show one buckwheat pancake cut into halves and another into quarters, demonstrating the same total.

explanation_text: Two small piles of husked corn combined into one pile simplify the count, just as a fraction is reduced to its simplest form.
image_prompt: Depict smaller piles of corn merging into one larger pile, labeled with reduced fractions.

yi_culture: Full and half baskets of grain
explanation_text: If you have 3 full baskets of grain and half a basket more, that is 3½, a whole number plus a fraction. This is a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full grain baskets and one half-full basket labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When husked corn fills more than one basket but is still counted in basketfuls, the amount is greater than one whole. That represents an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Show small woven baskets piled above one full level, symbolizing fractions greater than 1.

explanation_text: Combining rice from different bowls at the long street banquet shows how fractional amounts join to make a whole. Adding fractions combines parts of equal size.
image_prompt: Show rice from several small bowls being poured together into one total bowl.

explanation_text: Serving out part of a bowl of buckwheat porridge leaves a remainder, showing subtraction of a fractional part.
image_prompt: Show a bowl of buckwheat porridge with part being ladled out, the remainder labeled as the fraction left.

explanation_text: If each person takes half of a half portion of Yi flatbread, you are finding a fraction of a fraction. This is how multiplying fractions works.
image_prompt: Show flatbread divided into halves, and one half divided again to show smaller portions.

explanation_text: When a bamboo steamer of buckwheat cakes is split into equal smaller shares, you are dividing a fraction by another fraction. The total amount stays the same.
image_prompt: Show buckwheat cakes from a bamboo steamer being split into smaller even shares.

explanation_text: Water for the mountain terraces is measured in liters and parts of liters, such as 1.5 liters. Parts of a liter are written as decimals.
image_prompt: Show a measuring container marked with 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters of water for the terraces.

explanation_text: Saying half a basket or 0.5 basket describes the same amount of corn. Converting between fractions and decimals keeps the value the same.
image_prompt: Show two grain baskets, one marked ½ and another 0.5, holding the same amount.

explanation_text: When a student scores 87 out of 100 on an exam at school, that is 87%. Percents express parts out of one hundred.
image_prompt: Show an exam paper with 87/100 written and an 87% mark beside it.

explanation_text: A 20% discount on a woven bag at the Chuxiong market shows how to find a percent of a price. Percents help you compute parts of any amount.
image_prompt: Show a market sign with a woven bag marked 20% off and price tags with reduced amounts.

explanation_text: If some jars of pickled vegetables are not labeled, each unknown jar stands for an unknown amount. In math, such unknown amounts are variables.
image_prompt: Show labeled jars and one unlabeled jar marked as x.

explanation_text: If you have 2 full jars and x more unlabeled ones, the total is written as the expression 2 + x. Expressions combine known and unknown quantities.
image_prompt: Show two labeled jars plus one unlabeled jar, symbolized as 2 + x.

explanation_text: A carrying pole with baskets hangs level only when both sides weigh the same. Keeping both sides equal is exactly what an equation does.
image_prompt: Show a shoulder carrying pole with equal baskets on both sides, labeled as an equation.

explanation_text: When one side of a carrying pole is heavier, you add or remove weight to level it. Finding the missing weight solves a one-step equation.
image_prompt: Show a carrying pole with one heavy basket and one lighter basket, the missing weight marked as x.

explanation_text: To make buckwheat tea you first roast the grain, then pour hot water, each step depending on the one before. Solving a two-step equation also needs steps in order.
image_prompt: Show the step sequence: roast buckwheat, add water, then the tea, symbolizing step-by-step solving.

explanation_text: When one family's corn harvest is larger than another's, the amounts are not equal. Comparisons like greater than or less than are inequalities.
image_prompt: Show two harvest piles of corn of different sizes with > and < symbols between them.

explanation_text: To weave a cloth you must first set the warp threads and only then pass the weft. The order of steps matters, just like the order of operations in math.
image_prompt: Show a backstrap loom with the warp prepared before the weft is woven, labeled like parentheses and exponents.

explanation_text: If a worn shuttle is replaced by an identical one, the weaving continues unchanged. Replacing a variable with its value is substitution.
image_prompt: Show a worn shuttle replaced by an identical one, representing substitution.

explanation_text: Stars over the Stone Forest at night each mark a single position in the sky. A point in geometry marks a single location.
image_prompt: Show a night sky above karst towers with individual stars marked as points on a coordinate grid.

explanation_text: The straight ridgelines of the karst towers stretch on without end. A line in geometry is straight and extends in both directions.
image_prompt: Show straight lines traced along the tops of the karst peaks, representing geometric lines.

explanation_text: When a carved wooden door swings open, it makes an angle with its frame. An angle measures how far one line turns from another.
image_prompt: Show a carved wooden Yi door partially open with the angle clearly marked.

explanation_text: On the backstrap loom, warp and weft threads cross at right angles to form the cloth. Lines that meet at 90° are perpendicular.
image_prompt: Show backstrap loom threads crossing at right angles, marked with 90° symbols.

explanation_text: The rows of mountain terraces run side by side at equal distance and never meet. Such lines are parallel.
image_prompt: Show parallel rows of rice terraces running side by side across a hillside.

explanation_text: The diamond, square, and zigzag shapes in Yi embroidery are all closed figures with straight sides. Closed straight-sided figures are polygons.
image_prompt: Show Yi embroidered cloth with closed geometric shapes forming patterns.

explanation_text: The pointed summits of the Stone Forest towers trace triangular outlines. A triangle is a closed figure with three sides.
image_prompt: Show karst tower peaks with triangular outlines highlighted.

explanation_text: Square and rectangular motifs are common in Yi embroidery. A closed figure with four sides is a quadrilateral.
image_prompt: Show Yi embroidery patterns built from squares and rectangles.

explanation_text: Walking the whole boundary of a terraced field measures its perimeter. Perimeter is the distance around a shape.
image_prompt: Show a person walking the edge of a terraced field with a dashed boundary line.

explanation_text: The surface of an embroidered panel that the pattern covers is its area. Area measures the space inside a shape.
image_prompt: Show an embroidered cloth panel with its covered surface shaded to show area.

explanation_text: How much water a bamboo tube can hold is its volume. Volume measures the space inside a three-dimensional object.
image_prompt: Show bamboo tubes filled to different levels to illustrate volume.

explanation_text: The sun-and-moon motif painted on Torch Festival torches is a circle. From the center, the rim is a fixed distance called the radius, and twice that is the diameter.
image_prompt: Show a Torch Festival torch with a sun-and-moon motif, labeled with radius and diameter lines.

explanation_text: No matter the size of a round buckwheat flatbread, its circumference divided by its diameter is always about 3.14. This constant is π.
image_prompt: Show round buckwheat flatbreads labeled with circumference and diameter measurements.

explanation_text: The warp and weft threads of the backstrap loom cross to make a grid, and every crossing has a position. This is like a coordinate plane with axes.
image_prompt: Show a loom grid with warp and weft threads labeled as x and y axes.

explanation_text: Marking each game stall's spot in the village square on a map is like plotting points. Every stall has an x and y position.
image_prompt: Show a village square map with festival stalls marked as points at their coordinates.

explanation_text: The paired motifs in Yi embroidery mirror each other across a center line. When two halves match exactly, the design has symmetry.
image_prompt: Show a symmetrical Yi embroidery motif split by a mirror line.

explanation_text: During the sani dance, dancers turn, shift, and slide, changing position and direction. These movements resemble transformations in geometry.
image_prompt: Show sani dancers turning and shifting positions to illustrate transformations.

explanation_text: Making buckwheat noodles needs a fixed balance of flour to water. Comparing two quantities like 2 cups to 1 cup is a ratio.
image_prompt: Show bowls of buckwheat flour and water labeled with a 2:1 ratio.

explanation_text: When an embroidery pattern is enlarged for a bigger panel, every part is scaled by the same amount. Keeping the same relationship is a proportion.
image_prompt: Show a small and a large Yi embroidery pattern with the same geometric proportions.

explanation_text: If a hiker walks 4 kilometers each hour along the mountain paths, that is a unit rate. A unit rate compares an amount to one unit.
image_prompt: Show a hiker on a mountain path with speed measured as kilometers per hour.

explanation_text: Drawing the whole village on a small cloth with every distance shrunk by the same factor is a scale drawing. The map keeps the village's true proportions.
image_prompt: Show a village and a smaller scaled map side by side with a scale legend.

explanation_text: If a family's corn harvest grows from 500 to 600 jin, that is a 20% increase. Percent change measures how much a value grows or shrinks.
image_prompt: Show two harvest piles growing in size with a +20% label.

explanation_text: Each evening the herder counts the sheep and notes how many are white or black. Recording these counts is data collection.
image_prompt: Show a herder marking tallies of sheep on a wooden board.

explanation_text: Writing down how much grain each terrace produced each season lets a family compare the months. Tables and graphs organize such numbers.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph comparing terrace harvest across the four seasons.

explanation_text: Adding the corn of several baskets and dividing by the number of baskets gives the average. This average is called the mean.
image_prompt: Show a row of corn baskets with the average amount highlighted.

explanation_text: When families' harvests are arranged from smallest to largest, the harvest in the middle is the median. The median splits the data in half.
image_prompt: Show lined-up harvest amounts with the middle one highlighted as the median.

explanation_text: If most sheep in the village are black, then black is the most frequent value. The value that appears most often is the mode.
image_prompt: Show sheep of several colors with black as the most common.

explanation_text: The gap between the biggest and smallest terrace harvest is the range. Range shows how spread out the data is.
image_prompt: Show a chart with the highest and lowest harvest bars marked for range.

explanation_text: One bar for each family shows how many sheep it owns, making comparison quick. Bar graphs compare categories with bar lengths.
image_prompt: Show a bar graph labeled by family names with sheep counts.

explanation_text: Joining monthly temperature readings in the mountains with a line shows the trend. Line graphs show how a value changes over time.
image_prompt: Show a line graph labeled with months and mountain temperatures.

explanation_text: A circle divided into slices can show how the village fields are shared among buckwheat, corn, and potatoes. Pie charts show parts of a whole.
image_prompt: Show a pie chart divided into crop categories with percentages.

explanation_text: At the Torch Festival games, guessing which marked stick a player will draw relies on chance. The chance of an outcome is probability.
image_prompt: Show festival game sticks in a bamboo container with probability labels above each.

yi_culture: Cycles of the sun and moon calendar
explanation_text: The Yi sun-and-moon calendar repeats the same cycle of months year after year. A sequence that repeats in a fixed order is a pattern.
image_prompt: Show a calendar circle of the Yi sun-and-moon months with repeating cycle marks.

explanation_text: In the dance circle, each step number leads to exactly one place in the pattern. A rule that gives one output for each input is a function.
image_prompt: Show a dance diagram mapping each step number (input) to its position in the circle (output).
